title: SIR applies a decade of exclusion lessons perfected on welfare schemes
shows: Veena Naregal, Professor of Sociology at the Institute of Economic Growth, Delhi, argues that the SIR carries over to the vote a method the Commission first tried on voter rolls in 2015 and that was refined on welfare lists in the decade since, which she calls freeze-and-prune, where a past list is the test of present entitlement and correction is slow. She traces the 2015 drive to link voter cards with Aadhaar, the order of 20 March 2015 that froze each state's ration numbers at 2011 levels and told states to check ration lists against voter lists, and the health insurance scheme's fixed pool of 10.74 crore families from the 2011 Socio-Economic and Caste Census. She sets the 2003 revision, which used the existing roll as its base, against the SIR's reliance on a roll two decades old, and notes that the Commission certified a national roll of 96.88 crore electors in February 2024. She names four kinds of exclusion the SIR creates and points to unpublished software rules that flag logical discrepancies and unmapped electors for notice and deletion.
quote: The SIR now shows that a method built to freeze access to welfare has been extended to the vote, and now applies to every voter.
note: Published 29 October 2026 at 6:30 am IST and updated 4:50 pm, by Veena Naregal, described at its foot as Professor of Sociology at the Institute of Economic Growth, Delhi. The full text is served on the page and was read with curl on 30 October 2026. Every argument in the summary is the author's. Her SIR figures (13.37 crore missing from draft rolls by 1 September, about 65 lakh left off in Bihar) are as she gives them, and her account of the two Election Commissioners' objections and the 97 Goa voters is attributed in the piece to The Indian Express. The page carries embedded posts on X that are not part of her argument.

title: Deemed ineligible: On the Supreme Court and SIR
shows: The Hindu's editorial takes up Justice Joymalya Bagchi's question at the Delhi hearing of 28 October, whether an elector who was lax or did not respond to the enumeration form should lose the vote for ever, and calls the shift of the burden of enrolment from the state to the elector the central design flaw of the SIR. It gives the share of names left off the draft as shifted or absent as 55% in Bihar and 72% in the third phase, and says Karnataka's final roll is 64.5 lakh short of the projected adult population after about 84 lakh were marked shifted or absent and a net 8.2 lakh were added during claims. It recalls that in the 2002 to 2003 revision enumerators enrolled shifted voters at their new homes. It says no statute or rule allows a voter's eligibility to be judged by family size or the age gap with a parent, and asks the Court to go beyond extended deadlines, to put back electors wrongly left off the draft and to settle the questions over the Commission's conduct and the appointment of its members.
quote: This is the central design flaw of the SIR as it shifts the burden of enrolment from the state to the elector, including those who have voted before, and treats a mere change of address as ground for deletion.
note: Editorial, published 30 October 2026 at 12:20 am IST and updated 8:24 am. The page marks itself as not free to read, so it is marked as needing a subscription or sign-in. The full text was read from the article body the page carries in its structured data, with curl on 30 October 2026. The hearing it discusses is court-54. Its words for the Karnataka figure are 'deleted, marked as shifted or absent during enumeration', and those are names left off the draft. Its finding that Muslims were disproportionately flagged in Delhi refers to an earlier analysis by the paper.
